entries.summary: AWS engineers share kernel optimizations for fused Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models on Amazon SageMaker AI: Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization, Triton backend routing for FP8 quantization, and eliminating Triton JIT recompilation. Together they deliver up to 10% higher throughput and up to 9% faster Time to First Token on H200 GPUs.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a sparsely-activated architecture that scales large language model (LLM) capacity while keeping per-token compute low. Because its operations account for a large share of total compute time, inefficiencies there directly raise request latency and cost. Therefore, optimizing MoE operations through kernel engineering offers the largest opportunity for performance gains.

Fused MoE is a key optimization technique for the MoE architecture. A fused MoE system merges token routing, data shuffling, and specialized network calculations into a single batched operation on the GPU. This replaces executing those routing and expert computations as separate, sequential loop operations. While this provides latency advantages, it also brings complexity in kernel implementations and debugging capability. High GPU utilization for this architecture requires hardware-specific optimizations.

In this post, we describe the different kernel optimizations we implemented for fused MoE models and show you how you can benefit from this work. We used a representative MoE model as our primary example.

Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization

To maximize tensor processing throughput, the NVIDIA Hopper architecture relies on the Warp Group Matrix Multiply Accumulate (WGMMA) instruction protocol, which executes collectively across a cooperative warpgroup of 128 threads. This operand asymmetry is fundamentally an instruction set architecture (ISA)-level property. In the underlying 

wgmma.mma_async
assembly definition, the hardware fixes the matrix row dimension (M) at a constant scale of 64 to define its parallel thread-mapping topology. The column dimension (N) remains highly variable. Operand A strictly maps across this fixed M dimension (using registers or shared memory), and Operand B maps across the variable N dimension (through a shared memory descriptor). These operand slots are therefore structurally non-interchangeable. Consequently, peak hardware tile utilization is governed by these rigid shape encodings, requiring that the M dimension equals or exceeds 64 to prevent compute execution lanes from sitting idle.

This structural preference stems from how Hopper Tensor Cores partition memory blocks. The hardware enforces a fixed minimum layout shape for the leading dimension of the first operand, locking the block height to exactly 64 (M=64). When a mathematical matrix possesses a large, continuous leading dimension in this primary slot, Hopper’s internal hardware schedulers can cleanly map and distribute data across the physical computing grid.

This structural asymmetry becomes a severe performance bottleneck during the decode phase of MoE networks. In a standard MoE layer, the linear algebra governing expert computation is formulated using traditional matrix notation:

A[M,K] x B[K,N] —> C[M,N]

Where (M) represents the token row count (or batch size), (K) represents the hidden feature dimension, and (N) represents the expansive expert output dimension.

During the decode phase, the system processes only one token per user sequence at a time. Consequently, the batch space or token row size is profoundly thin, regularly dropping to a profile where (M < 64), and frequently down to a single row (M = 1). Under this standard structural layout:

Matrix (A) transforms into a thin, fragmented horizontal vector (for example, 1 x 4096).

Matrix (B) (the core expert weights) remains in a large, dense vertical block (for example, 4096 x 8192).

Because the row count (M) is tiny, Matrix (A) is physically incapable of filling the hardware’s fixed (64)-row layout bucket for Operand A. When the WGMMA instruction executes over this layout, it leaves a vast portion of the physical Tensor Core capacity completely starved. The silicon spends clock cycles processing empty spatial slots, leading to poor hardware utilization.

In a standard dense LLM layer, weight matrices are static, unified, and perfectly contiguous. In an MoE layer, however, the workload is fractured across a fleet of independent subnetworks (experts). This creates unique memory and layout bottlenecks that make it hypersensitive to the WGMMA constraints of the Hopper GPU. In a standard dense layer, matrix multiplication multiplies a token vector by a single layer weight matrix. The output dimension (N) is the model’s hidden size (for example, 4096).

In a Fused MoE kernel, the GPU isn’t only multiplying against one expert. It’s grouping and running math for all active experts simultaneously to avoid launching individual kernels for each expert. For a standard dense layer, N is the hidden size (4,096). For a fused MoE layer, N is the number of experts chosen multiplied by the expert intermediate size. For a model running a 

topk=8
routine, the effective N dimension inside the fused kernel explodes into tens or hundreds of thousands of parameters. Because the N dimension is so disproportionately large compared to the tiny decode token size (M=1), the layout asymmetry becomes extreme. Transposing the matrices moves this large, combined MoE dimension into the primary slot, unlocking hardware prefetching at a scale that standard dense layers cannot match.

To resolve this hardware misalignment without altering the underlying mathematical integrity of the model, we exploit the algebraic property of matrix transposition:

BT[N,K] x AT[K,M] —> CT[N,M]

By programmatically flipping the matrix multiplication before it reaches the PTX assembly layer, we realigned the software to match the exact topography of the Hopper silicon. This transposition triggers two immediate architectural advantages on the GPU. First, it saturates the physical layout. The expansive expert dimension (N = 8192) is promoted to the first operand position (BT), and because (N) is large it easily floods the hardware’s mandatory (64)-row threshold. The Tensor Cores then operate at maximum local density with no wasted execution cycles. Second, it activates asynchronous prefetching. Hopper’s dedicated hardware copy engines can prefetch memory addresses asynchronously from shared memory straight into registers before the math execution block fires. Placing the continuous, large weight blocks (BT) in the leading slot lets these engines trace the data layout smoothly and keep the compute pipeline saturated without CPU intervention. This produced a 2–4 percent end-to-end output throughput improvement across large-scale MoE models on H200. We upstreamed this optimization to vLLM, and it is available in version 0.24.0 or later.

Backend routing for FP8 tensor quantization

Beyond kernel internals, the choice of which backend executes the MoE computation has a large effect on performance. The vLLM MoE oracle routes different quantization schemes to Triton, FlashInfer+CUTLASS, or other backends. Profiling revealed that for FP8 tensor-quantized models on Hopper, the Triton backend consistently outperforms the default 

FLASHINFER_CUTLASS
path.

The Triton backend outperforms CUTLASS in low-concurrency MoE workloads primarily because it replaces rigid, framework-level matrix math configurations with custom, operator-level register fusion. CUTLASS relies on standard C++ template structures that treat FP8 tensor scaling, matrix multiplication, and expert aggregation as discrete mathematical operations. The Triton backend instead consolidates this entire pipeline into a single hardware pass. Data is pulled from global high-bandwidth memory (HBM) exactly once and processed entirely within the GPU’s ultra-fast local SRAM registers and compute execution files. It’s then streamed back to the final matrix destination. This removes the slow global VRAM read/write roundtrips that compromise CUTLASS when it is forced to constantly step through intermediate tensor scaling steps.

Furthermore, this register-level fusion is specifically paired with dynamic scheduling layouts designed around variable token bucketing, resolving a severe structural flaw in traditional compilation templates. CUTLASS is natively optimized for dense, large, and predictable matrix dimensions. When it encounters the fluid, ultra-thin batch profiles (M < 64 or M = 1) typical of the live decode generation phase, its default block-tiling and thread-mapping structures become profoundly inefficient. The result is heavy warp under-utilization or expensive memory padding overhead. Conversely, the Triton MoE backend excels at dynamically mapping these small, fragmented token arrays across the physical boundaries of the active expert weights. This keeps the hardware’s internal prefetch streams and Tensor Core pipelines fully saturated even when processing highly unstable workloads at very low batch sizes.

Updating the routing policy is a pure configuration change with no kernel code modified. Still, it yielded a 10 percent end-to-end throughput improvement for FP8 quantized fused MoE models on H200. This improvement is available in the AWS Large Model Inference (LMI) v28 container.

Triton JIT recompilation elimination

One of the most impactful performance pathologies in GPU inference is also one of the least obvious: unnecessary kernel recompilation. Triton, the compiler framework underlying many of vLLM’s custom kernels, specializes integer arguments by default. Every time a kernel is invoked with a previously unseen value for a specialized parameter, Triton triggers a fresh just-in-time (JIT) compilation. In serving workloads where sequence lengths and batch sizes vary continuously, this creates a steady stream of compilation overhead that inflates latency, particularly Time to First Token (TTFT).

In MoE model serving, the 

_fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant_per_head
kernel (responsible for fused rotary position embedding and FP8 quantization) was recompiling on every new 
num_tokens
value. Adding 
do_not_specialize
annotations to the variable-length parameters removed these recompilations entirely, improving TTFT by 9 percent on H200 at 8-way tensor parallelism (PR #42849).

In a multi-GPU cluster, all 8 GPUs must execute their kernels in perfect, microsecond-level synchronization. If even one GPU must stop to recompile its local 

_fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant_per_head
kernel because its local token batch count changed, the other seven GPUs sit idle and wait for it. By eliminating recompilations across the entire cluster, we smoothed out the multi-GPU coordination overhead, delivering a 9 percent speedup for the user’s initial response latency. The principle here is to treat the compiler as a first-class optimization surface. Understanding how Triton specializes semantics and recognizing when parameters are dead or variable unlocks latency improvements with minimal code change.

We upstreamed this optimization to vLLM, and it is available in version 0.22.0 or later.

Conclusion

Through our collaboration with the vLLM community, we implemented and open sourced multiple kernel optimizations for fused MoE models. We apply these optimizations in the LMI Deep Learning Container on Amazon SageMaker AI. Together, these optimizations have delivered up to 10 percent higher throughput and up to 9 percent faster TTFT. To get started with custom model hosting, see the Amazon SageMaker AI hosting documentation.

entries.title: Accessing OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock with global cross-Region inference in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan
entries.summary: Learn how to run OpenAI GPT-6 Sol, Luna, and Astra on Amazon Bedrock through global cross-Region inference from Singapore, Jakarta, Thailand, Malaysia, and Taipei. This post covers the Converse and OpenAI-compatible APIs, IAM and SCP permissions, quota sizing, and monitoring inference from your source Region.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Accessing OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock with global cross-Region inference in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan

Single-Region inference can throttle when demand exceeds local capacity. Teams in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan need access to the newest OpenAI models beyond that capacity. Amazon Bedrock offers OpenAI GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna through global cross-Region inference from all five AWS Regions, and GPT-6 Astra from Asia Pacific (Singapore). This post shows you how to configure the call, set permissions, and monitor inference from your source Region.

GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6 Astra are all available through global cross-Region inference from the preceding Regions, on the 

bedrock-runtime
endpoint. See Cross-Region inference in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. For the full list of source and destination Regions in each profile, see Supported Regions and models for inference profiles.

In this post, we introduce the global cross-Region inference profiles and invoke them from Asia Pacific (Singapore) using the Converse API, the OpenAI-compatible APIs, and coding clients. We then cover the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and service control policy (SCP) configuration, quota management, and monitoring.

Global cross-Region inference profiles for OpenAI GPT-6

The GPT-6 family offers three models, each available through global cross-Region inference.

  • GPT-6 Sol brings strong reasoning and coding capabilities to complex tasks performed throughout the week.
  • GPT-6 Luna makes focused, repeatable tasks practical at high volume.
  • GPT-6 Astra handles complex reasoning, coding, and long-document work.

All three accept text and image input, client-side tool use, and prompt caching. They differ on reasoning effort. GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna accept none, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. GPT-6 Astra accepts the same levels except none. For GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, see Bring more intelligence to everyday work with GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna on Amazon Bedrock. For GPT-6 Astra, see Take on your most ambitious work with GPT-6 Astra on Amazon Bedrock.

Global cross-Region inference routes requests across supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed, giving you broad access to Amazon Bedrock capacity. You invoke it by passing a global cross-Region inference profile ID in place of a model ID. Your source Region is where you make the API call. Amazon Bedrock selects the destination Region for processing. Billing, quota tracking, AWS CloudTrail, and Amazon CloudWatch all stay in your source Region.

The following table lists the global cross-Region inference profile IDs and the source Regions covered in this post.

Global cross-Region inference profilesSource RegionsDestination Regions

global.openai.gpt-6-sol

global.openai.gpt-6-luna

Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1

Asia Pacific (Jakarta) ap-southeast-3

Asia Pacific (Malaysia) ap-southeast-5

Asia Pacific (Thailand) ap-southeast-7

Asia Pacific (Taipei) ap-east-2

 Supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed
global.openai.gpt-6-astraAsia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1Supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed

Inference profile availability and Region support change as AWS adds Regions and profiles, so confirm both on the model card before you build: GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6 Astra. For per-token rates, see Amazon Bedrock pricing.

Getting started with OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock

Start with the prerequisites, then invoke any of the three profiles through the Converse API, the OpenAI-compatible APIs, or your existing coding client.

Prerequisites

  • An IAM identity with permission to invoke the profile. The IAM policy in the Security and permissions section grants only what these examples need.
  • Your source Region activated. Only the Region you call from needs activating. You do not activate destination Regions, which run on Amazon Bedrock managed capacity. Singapore (
    ap-southeast-1
    ) is a Region that is enabled by default. Jakarta (
    ap-southeast-3
    ), Malaysia (
    ap-southeast-5
    ), Thailand (
    ap-southeast-7
    ), and Taipei (
    ap-east-2
    ) are opt-in Regions you must activate first. For more information, see Enable or disable AWS Regions in your account.
  • A current AWS SDK or CLI. The OpenAI-compatible examples also require the OpenAI SDK and the Amazon Bedrock token generator. Install them with 
    pip install boto3 openai aws-bedrock-token-generator
    .

The Amazon Bedrock console lists all three global cross-Region inference profiles under system-defined inference profiles. See Figure 1.

Invoke GPT-6 models through Amazon Bedrock Runtime

Each model supports three access paths on this endpoint: the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, the OpenAI Responses API, and the OpenAI Chat Completions API. The OpenAI-compatible APIs are called on the 

/openai/v1
paths rather than through the AWS SDKs, and the endpoint accepts either Signature Version 4 (SigV4) or an Amazon Bedrock API key. Pass the global cross-Region inference profile ID as the 
model
in every case.

Converse API. This example calls GPT-6 Sol from Asia Pacific (Singapore) and logs the response. Set 

BEDROCK_PROFILE_ID
to 
global.openai.gpt-6-luna
or 
global.openai.gpt-6-astra
to switch models, or call 
converse_stream
for streaming.

OpenAI Chat Completions API. Point the OpenAI SDK at the Regional endpoint and pass the same profile ID.

When migrating an existing OpenAI client:

  • Set the model parameter on every request, including those referencing a previous response.
  • Use supported tool types: 
    function
    , 
    mcp
    , 
    custom
    , 
    namespace
    , and 
    tool_search
    .
  • Configure the inference profile ID directly in your client rather than querying the models endpoint.

Set up the ChatGPT desktop app and Codex CLI

The ChatGPT desktop app and the Codex CLI share 

~/.codex/config.toml
, so one change covers both. Of the two built-in Amazon Bedrock providers, only 
amazon-bedrock-runtime
accepts an inference profile.

SigV4 signing means there is no key to rotate. Add 

profile = ""
for a non-default profile, and set 
region
explicitly, because the client otherwise falls back to 
AWS_REGION
. Substitute another profile ID for 
model
to change models.

Codex reports a 272,000-token window for these profiles, which is its own bundled figure rather than a service limit. Raise it with 

model_context_window
. This configuration needs Codex CLI 0.148 or later.

Figure 2 shows the result in the app.

Security and permissions

Amazon Bedrock offers a range of controls over inference. Two of them matter here. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies control which roles can invoke which profiles, and service control policies (SCPs) apply organization-wide controls, including Region scope. This section covers both, and where request data lands.

IAM permissions for global cross-Region inference

To call any of these models through a global cross-Region inference profile, your IAM policy needs four statements:

  • Access to the inference profile and the project/default resource in your source Region.
  • Access to the foundation model in your source Region, scoped to the inference profile.
  • The Region-agnostic Amazon Resource Name (ARN) for the foundation model, 
    arn:aws:bedrock:::foundation-model/openai.gpt-6-sol
    , with 
    aws:RequestedRegion
    set to 
    unspecified
    to permit cross-Region routing.
  • bedrock:CallWithBearerToken
    for API-key authentication.

This IAM policy grants permission to invoke GPT-6 Sol through global cross-Region inference from 

ap-southeast-1
. Replace with your AWS account ID and 
ap-southeast-1
with your source Region.

If you use streaming (

converse_stream
or 
stream=True
), add 
bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream
to the Action in the first three statements. Converse authorizes as 
bedrock:InvokeModel
. If you only call Converse with SigV4 credentials, drop the fourth statement.

To switch models, replace 

openai.gpt-6-sol
with 
openai.gpt-6-luna
or 
openai.gpt-6-astra
throughout. For the complete reference, see IAM policy requirements for global cross-Region inference.

Service control policy considerations for global cross-Region inference

A global cross-Region inference request carries no Region name. Amazon Bedrock sets 

aws:RequestedRegion
to 
unspecified
, so a Region allowlist in an SCP denies the call, and the error names only the policy type, not which policy. That is a common reason a first call fails in an enterprise account.

Rather than widening the allowlist, scope the exception. Amazon Bedrock populates the 

bedrock:InferenceProfileArn
condition key during authorization, so an SCP can allow these profiles while keeping Region controls for everything else. The following SCP does that.

The first statement enforces your Region allowlist for every service except Amazon Bedrock inference. The second denies that inference outside those Regions unless it routes through a global cross-Region inference profile. For geographic profiles, add their prefix (for example 

inference-profile/us.*
) to the 
ArnNotLike
list, because geographic requests carry a real Region name. Keep your source Region in the allowlist, and add the global services your organization uses to 
NotAction
.

A blunter alternative is to add 

unspecified
to your existing allowlist, which works but opens the same exception to every other service. For a ready-to-use policy file, see the aws-samples service-control-policy-examples repository.

Data retention and abuse detection

For automated offline abuse detection, classifier-flagged traffic is retained by AWS for up to 30 days and processed programmatically. Under cross-Region inference that retention happens in the destination Region, which for a global profile is any supported commercial AWS Region where the model is deployed. Eligible customers might request full zero data retention through their AWS account team. For more information, see Amazon Bedrock abuse detection and Data retention.

If your organization has data residency requirements, take this to your risk and compliance team early. See the AWS Financial Services Compliance Center country pages for these five countries. We recommend you obtain your own advice on compliance with the requirements relevant to your business.

Quota management

GPT-6 quotas on 

bedrock-runtime
are measured in tokens per minute (TPM), tracked against the source Region you call from. Input and cache-write tokens count 1:1, and each output token consumes 10 tokens of quota. For example, a request with 2,000 input tokens and 1,000 output tokens depletes 12,000 tokens from your quota.

Amazon Bedrock reserves the full 

max_tokens
up front, so set it close to the completions you expect. One quota covers 
InvokeModel
, Converse, Responses, and Chat Completions. Review and raise it on the Service Quotas console from your source Region. Before production, request increases early and alarm on 
EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage
in the 
AWS/Bedrock
namespace at 70–80 percent of your allocation. See How tokens are counted in Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock endpoints and quotas for current values.

Monitoring and logging

Your operational surface stays in your source Region. Amazon CloudWatch metrics, AWS CloudTrail events, model invocation logs, quota accounting, and billing all remain in the Region you called from. You pay that Region’s rates, not the processing Region’s.

CloudTrail records where each request was processed. AWS documents a global cross-Region inference profile’s destinations as its commercial Regions rather than enumerating them. 

GetInferenceProfile
returns the Region-agnostic and source-Region model ARNs rather than a destination list. Your per-request record is 
additionalEventData.inferenceRegion
in CloudTrail in your source Region. Inference on this endpoint is a management event, logged by default at no extra cost. CloudTrail Event History retains 90 days, so longer horizons need a trail or model invocation logging. Retrieve the CloudTrail events with this command.

Set the window around a call you just made, because CloudTrail delivery lags by a few minutes. If the most recent event was a failed call, it carries an 

errorCode
and no 
inferenceRegion
. Raise 
--max-results
and pick an event without 
errorCode
.

Metrics and coding-agent usage stay in CloudWatch. Where developers reach GPT-6 through a coding agent, CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights adds ready-made dashboards under GenAI Observability that break token use down by user, team, and cost center. The agents emit OpenTelemetry metrics natively. For Codex, see Set up OpenTelemetry for OpenAI Codex.

Clean up

This post adds an IAM policy and optionally an SCP statement and a logging destination. Detach or delete the IAM policy you attached, and revert the SCP entry if you added one. Delete the model invocation logging destination in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs if you created one, to avoid storage charges. The global cross-Region inference profiles are system-defined, so there is nothing to delete.

Conclusion

This post showed how to invoke GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna from five Asia Pacific source Regions, and GPT-6 Astra from Asia Pacific (Singapore), through global cross-Region inference on 

bedrock-runtime
. Pass a global cross-Region inference profile ID as the 
model
parameter, and configure the IAM policy and SCP exception from this post. The same endpoint serves the OpenAI-compatible APIs, so an existing OpenAI integration moves across by changing a base URL and a key.

To get started, attach the IAM policy from this post, and send a first request through 

global.openai.gpt-6-sol
. Size your tokens-per-minute quota at the 10x burndown rate, and confirm in CloudTrail that 
additionalEventData.inferenceRegion
appears on your calls.

For more information, see the Amazon Bedrock User Guide, Route model inference requests across AWS Regions with cross-Region inference, and Amazon Bedrock pricing.

entries.title: Deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI
entries.summary: Learn how to deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI. This technical how-to serves OpenAI-compatible chat completions with the AWS Deep Learning Container for llama.cpp, then extends the runtime with SemIf to return probabilities over declared options on CPU or GPU.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI

Applications that route requests, select agent actions, or assign policy outcomes often need scores over a fixed set of choices instead of free-form text. Deploying these decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI gives you a managed path for serving quantized models on CPU or GPU infrastructure.

This post continues a series on specialized AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) for generative AI inference. Previous posts cover WhisperX, vLLM-Omni – Part 1, and vLLM-Omni – Part 2.

In this post, you first use the AWS DLC for llama.cpp to serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through SageMaker AI 

InvokeEndpoint
. You then extend the same runtime with SemIf, formerly OpenJev, which returns probabilities over declared options without decoding an answer token. The accompanying code sample includes CPU and GPU deployment options.

Solution overview

Figure 1 shows two deployment paths from the same packaged model. The text-generation path uses the AWS DLC for llama.cpp and returns generated responses through the OpenAI-compatible API. The structured-decision path builds a child image that replaces the default server with a SemIf adapter and returns probabilities for declared options.

For the standard path, package the model as 

model.tar.gz
in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and reference the published DLC image directly. The container finds the first 
.gguf
file under 
/opt/ml/model
, maps 
POST /invocations
to 
llama-server
at 
/v1/chat/completions
, and passes 
SM_LLAMA_CPP_*
environment variables to llama.cpp arguments.

The 

llama-server
HTTP API doesn’t expose the final-position logits and state operations that SemIf uses. The structured-decision path therefore uses AWS CodeBuild to build a child image and store it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). The child image keeps the DLC’s compiled CPU or CUDA libraries while replacing its entry point with a SageMaker-compatible adapter.

Understand the input and output schemas

The AWS DLC for llama.cpp accepts the OpenAI Chat Completions schema. Send a 

messages
array with 
role
and 
content
, plus generation controls such as 
max_tokens
and 
stream
:

The response uses the OpenAI-compatible 

choices
array. Read generated text from 
choices[0].message.content
.

SemIf uses a constrained decision schema instead of chat messages. The request contains a caller-defined ID, unstructured state, a question, and an ordered list of allowed options:

The response returns 

option_ids
, 
probabilities
, and raw 
option_logits
in the same order, along with prompt, timing, and pinned model metadata. With stable option IDs, your application can apply thresholds, fallbacks, and policy checks without parsing generated prose.

SemIf belongs to a broader class of decision models that score application-defined outcomes from unstructured state. Other implementations include Jev, TypeSafe’s decision model and 

/v1/systemone
API; Kev, a model server designed for TypeSafe API compatibility; and Strands Decider 2B, a purpose-built model for agent workflows with calibrated outputs.

Choose the right decision workflows

Use this pattern when your application defines the allowed choices at request time and needs a model to interpret unstructured context. Examples include routing a case to a queue, extracting one value from a known set, assigning an incident priority, checking a policy outcome, or selecting an agent action. Keep authorization and deterministic business rules outside the model, and validate model probabilities before treating them as operational confidence.

Use the standard SageMaker AI text-generation path when you need OpenAI-compatible chat completions through 

InvokeEndpoint
. The SageMaker AI image maps 
POST /invocations
to the 
llama-server
/v1/chat/completions
endpoint. Build a child image only when your application needs behavior that this interface doesn’t provide, such as SemIf’s direct logits and state access.

Removing answer-token generation doesn’t remove model inference. The model still processes the complete state, question, and option descriptions before SemIf reads the final logits. Keep prompts focused, and evaluate the selected model with labeled decisions from your application before production use.

Tune for your latency and quality targets

The following benchmark applies to the SemIf extension, not the text-generation endpoint. Model size, quantization, prompt length, runtime, and CPU thread count affect each decision. To quantify these trade-offs, we sent the same 231 public JevBench tasks serially to one CPU endpoint and one GPU endpoint.

ConfigurationAWS DLC for llama.cppValid responsesAccuracyClient p50Client p95
Qwen3.5-4B 
Q4_K_M
, 
ml.c6i.8xlarge
, 32 threads		 llama-cpp:server-sagemaker-cpu-v1 231/231179/231 (77.5%)1.715 seconds19.291 seconds
Qwen3.5-4B 
Q4_K_M
, 
ml.g6e.xlarge
, full GPU offload		 llama-cpp:server-sagemaker-cuda-v1 231/231180/231 (77.9%)0.352 seconds0.599 seconds

Compared with the CPU configuration, the GPU endpoint was 4.9 times faster at p50 and 32.2 times faster at p95. The sample uses the SageMaker AI instance pools feature to list compatible GPU instance types in priority order, so SageMaker can select an alternative when the first preference isn’t available. The pool ordered 

g6e
, 
g6
, 
g5
, then 
g4dn
. SageMaker selected 
ml.g6e.xlarge
, and startup logs confirmed that llama.cpp offloaded all 34 model layers to an NVIDIA L40S. The CPU and GPU images used different llama.cpp builds and produced different predictions on six hard tasks. Treat the one-answer accuracy difference as runtime variation, not evidence that GPU offload improves model quality.

Smaller models reduced median latency, but the 2B and 0.8B candidates achieved 66.7 percent and 58.4 percent accuracy. The sample therefore keeps the 4B 

Q4_K_M
model as its quality-first default. These measurements include network latency and aren’t service guarantees.

Benchmark the complete model and infrastructure configuration against your own decisions. Use CPU for background, offline, or low-throughput workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive and can tolerate seconds of response time. Use GPU for interactive decisions, long prompts, or workloads with tight tail-latency targets. Keep state and option descriptions concise, group decisions that share the same state into one request, and scale endpoint instances for concurrency. Shared-state scoring reuses the common prompt prefix, while the adapter returns retryable HTTP 

503
responses instead of allowing an unbounded queue around its stateful llama.cpp context.

Prerequisites

You need:

  • An AWS account and an S3 bucket in your deployment AWS Region.
  • Python 3.10 or later, Git, and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).

entries.title: Run multi-node inference workloads using Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers
entries.summary: Learn how to deploy one large language model across two GPU nodes on Amazon EKS using the multi-node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers, with separate prefill and decode nodes behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The pre-built container ships the full inference stack, so you configure the deployment instead of assembling it.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Run multi-node inference workloads using Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers

This post shows how to deploy one large language model (LLM) across two GPU nodes on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with the multi-node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers. It uses separate prefill and decode nodes behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. This kind of multi-node setup is common for tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism, as well as prefill/decode disaggregation inference workloads. In a previous post, we introduced the Ray Serve DLC and used it to stand up a small model behind an HTTP endpoint on a single GPU node. You had a working inference endpoint, and the container keeps the GPU stack compatible, including CUDA libraries, so you did not need to write boilerplate code.

Ray is a distributed compute framework, so Ray Serve deployments can span multiple nodes. Customers use multi-node Ray Serve for several reasons. Some want to run foundation or open-weight models that are too large for a single GPU. Others need more throughput than one replica can deliver. Still others want to separate the two phases of inference to improve performance. In each case, customers must build the dependency chain themselves: choosing compatible libraries for the GPU stack and debugging issues when a component drifts out of alignment. This is undifferentiated work that takes time and effort away from delivering models.

AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) have long solved this kind of problem for training and inferencing workloads. DLCs are pre-built, performance-optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately. With the launch of the Ray LLM DLC for multi-node deployments, that same approach now extends to multi-node inference. You get a container purpose-built for serving models behind an HTTP endpoint, maintained and tested by AWS, with the full inference stack already assembled.

This post walks through implementing multi-node disaggregated inference using multi-node Ray LLM DLC: deploying a single large language model across two GPU-powered nodes on Amazon EKS cooperating behind a single endpoint. While one of the GPU nodes handles the prefill phase, the other GPU node handles the decode phase. Separating the phases prevents compute-heavy long prompts from stalling token generation for requests already in progress. This approach is well suited for workloads such as Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), document summarization, and agentic applications. We use the multi-node Ray LLM DLC, which ships Ray Serve LLM, NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library (NIXL), and the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) stack, and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with no application code. The complete code is available in the accompanying repository.

Why prefill/decode (PD) disaggregation

LLM inference has two distinct phases. Prefill processes the entire input prompt in parallel and builds the key-value (KV) cache. Decode then generates the response one token at a time, reading and extending that cache. Prefill is compute bound, and Decode is bound by memory bandwidth. When both phases share one GPU, they contend for the same resources, and the bursty, compute-heavy prefill work interferes with the steady, latency-sensitive decode work. Separating the prefill phase from the decode phase means you can select the hardware and serving properties for each phase, improving overall performance at scale.

PD disaggregation places the two phases on separate nodes, so each phase runs without interfering with the other and can be scaled independently. The trade-off is that the KV cache built during prefill must be handed to the decode node, and that transfer should be fast enough not to erase the benefit. That is exactly why the interconnect between the nodes matters.

What the Ray LLM DLC provides

AWS DLCs are pre-built, performance-optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately. All components are validated together before each release, so there is no version drift between the CUDA runtime, the framework, and the serving layer. Security patches are applied at build time.

The Ray LLM DLC extends this to distributed LLM serving. It ships vLLM as the inference engine, Ray Serve’s HTTP as the serving layer, NIXL for KV-cache transfer between nodes, and the EFA stack (libfabric and aws-ofi-nccl) for high-bandwidth node-to-node communication. Because the Ray Serve LLM library includes a built-in application builder, the entire serving application is a block of YAML. There’s no handler class, no model archiver, and no custom image to build. A single helper, 

build_pd_openai_app
, takes a prefill configuration and a decode configuration and wires the KV-cache transfer between them behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Architecture

The following diagram shows how the deployment is laid out on Amazon EKS. A user request reaches the Ray head on the CPU system node, and the two GPU worker nodes run the prefill and decode phases of the model.

The deployment is an EKS cluster inside a virtual private cloud (VPC). Nodes run in private subnets with outbound access through a NAT Gateway. A CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) hosts system workloads, the KubeRay operator, and the Ray head pod, which is CPU-only. Two GPU worker nodes (g6.8xlarge) run the Ray workers: one serving the prefill phase, and the other serving the decode phase. Both nodes pull the Ray LLM DLC from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR).

KubeRay watches the RayService you apply and wires the head-to-worker join automatically. Ray Serve places the prefill and decode deployments on the two GPU workers. The KV cache flows from the prefill worker to the decode worker over NIXL, using EFA through NIXL’s libfabric backend. The GPU node group is pinned to a single Availability Zone (AZ) because EFA cannot cross AZs.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this post, you need:

  • An AWS account with billing enabled.
  • Sufficient service quota for running two g6.8xlarge instances (at least 64 vCPU) in your target Region.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) with credentials configured.
  • kubectl CLI for communicating with a Kubernetes cluster’s control plane.
  • eksctl CLI for creating and managing clusters on EKS.
  • helm (package manager for Kubernetes) to install KubeRay operator.
  • envsubst utility (part of the GNU gettext) to render the manifest.

Verify that your AWS credentials are active with the following command:

Use the pre-built application to serve inference

The application is the 

serveConfigV2
block in 
manifest/rayservice.yaml
. It uses 
build_pd_openai_app
, which takes a 
prefill_config
and a 
decode_config
and connects the KV-cache transfer between them:

A few settings carry most of the weight. 

max_model_len: 4096
sizes the context to fit the measured KV cache on the GPU. 
dtype: bfloat16
and 
gpu_memory_utilization: 0.90
set precision and how much VRAM vLLM can claim. 
enforce_eager: true
skips CUDA graph capture to reduce peak GPU memory (model- and input-dependent). The 
kv_transfer_config
setting is what makes disaggregation work: both phases use 
NixlConnector
with 
kv_role: kv_both
and a distinct 
engine_id
(prefill on one, decode on the other). The critical setting is 
kv_connector_extra_config: { backends: ["LIBFABRIC"] }
. Without that line, NIXL defaults to UCX, which runs at TCP speed even on EFA.

The rest of the manifest, in 

rayClusterConfig
, describes the pods. The head pod is CPU-only (
num-gpus: "0"
) and pinned to the system node group. Each worker pod requests one GPU and one EFA interface (
nvidia.com/gpu: "1", vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1"
) and targets the GPU nodes through 
nodeSelector: { role: gpu-worker }
. It runs 
privileged: true
because NIXL registers CUDA VRAM with the EFA NIC. The 
IPC_LOCK
capability alone isn’t enough. The workers set 
FI_PROVIDER=efa
, read 
VLLM_HOST_IP
from the pod IP, and mount a shared-memory volume. Memory limits sit well above the roughly 18 GiB checkpoint so the OS page cache can hold it. For Qwen3.5-9B model loading on g6.8xlarge with the preceding cache configuration, the model weights loading drops from around 145 seconds to about 2 seconds on restart.

Deploy on Amazon EKS

All scripts share a single configuration file, 

scripts/env.sh
. The script contains defaults for 
CLUSTER_NAME
, 
REGION
, 
K8S_VERSION
, and 
NAMESPACE
. Other defaults cover the system and GPU node groups, the KubeRay version, and the model. Override any variable by exporting it before running a script.

From the project root, set a base directory, then load the variables:

Step 1: Create the EKS cluster

This provisions the EKS cluster (VPC, OIDC provider, core add-ons) and a CPU system node group that runs system workloads, the KubeRay operator, and the Ray head. Nodes run in private subnets with egress through a NAT Gateway, and cluster subnets are placed in the AZs that offer the GPU instance type. The script is idempotent and takes 15–20 minutes on a fresh run.

Step 2: Add GPU worker nodes

This creates the GPU node group: two g6.8xlarge instances with EFA enabled, pinned to a single AZ and labeled 

role=gpu-worker
so the Ray workers target them. Enabling EFA also installs the EFA device plugin, which advertises 
vpc.amazonaws.com/efa
on each node. This step takes about 5-20 minutes, usually longer on a first run.

Step 3: Install the KubeRay operator

This installs the KubeRay operator using Helm, pinned to the system node group to keep the GPU nodes available for inference. KubeRay watches the RayService you apply next and wires the head-to-worker join automatically. This step takes about 1–2 minutes.

Step 4: Deploy the RayService

This renders 

manifest/rayservice.yaml
with your image, model, and naming variables using envsubst and applies it. KubeRay creates the head and two worker pods, and Ray Serve LLM brings up the prefill and decode deployments. The script waits for the head to be Ready, both workers to be Running, and finally for the Serve app to report RUNNING. Because each node loads the model, expect this step to take several minutes.

Check status at any time, including which node each pod landed on and the GPU capacity available:

Invoke the model

After the Serve app is healthy, KubeRay creates a stable 

-serve-svc
Service. Port-forward to it:

Because the DLC exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, you can list models and send a standard chat-completion request with no custom schema:

Verify EFA is being used

NIXL falls back to a TCP-speed transport if it cannot use libfabric, and it does so without raising an error, so it’s worth confirming the backend it picked. Grep the worker logs:

deploy_node_group.sh
already prints the 
vpc.amazonaws.com/efa
count per node when it creates the group. For a cross-node bandwidth number, the DLC ships a prebuilt NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) benchmark at 
/usr/local/bin/all_reduce_perf
.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, tear down the resources in reverse order:

Conclusion and next steps

You served a single model across two GPU nodes with prefill/decode disaggregation, and the entire application was a block of YAML, with no handler code, no model archiver, and no hand-assembled GPU and EFA stack. The multi-node Ray LLM DLC supplied the tested inference stack, KubeRay orchestrated the Ray cluster, and NIXL over EFA carried the KV cache between nodes. Your job was to configure it, not to build it.

Common patterns for running multi-node inference include tensor and pipeline parallelism (sharding a model too big for one instance), data parallelism (replicating a model for throughput), and prefill/decode disaggregation (separating the two phases of inference onto different nodes).

From here you can scale the decode replicas for more throughput, move to larger models with tensor or pipeline parallelism on larger GPU instances, or layer extra libraries onto the same tested base for models that need them. For the full code, the current list of image tags, and the underlying mechanics, see the accompanying repository, the Ray LLM DLC available images page, the Ray Serve LLM prefill/decode documentation, and the EFA documentation.

entries.title: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in September 2026
entries.summary: A monthly recap of the latest Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Strands updates from September 2026: broader model choice, faster serverless agents with built-in evaluation, and automated knowledge base syncing with native enterprise connectors.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in September 2026

A recap of the latest Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Strands updates from September 2026

At AWS, we believe the fastest path to enterprise AI is giving builders real choice at every layer: model, runtime, and tooling. That belief shapes how we invest across Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore, and Strands. Amazon Bedrock continues expanding access to leading frontier models so you can build and scale AI applications securely. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides the managed infrastructure to build, connect, and deploy enterprise agents using any framework or model. Strands gives you an open source toolkit to build agents and run anywhere.

As AI models become more capable and model choice expands, the industry conversations are shifting. Model performance is no longer the only question. Customers now weigh cost against benefit for their specific use case, and those decisions matter when delegating work to agents in production. AI agents are already moving into workflows that require them to reason over enterprise knowledge, operate across long-horizon tasks, and act in systems where security, accuracy, and governance matter. The focus is now shifting beyond the model itself to the broader system around it, including the context agents can access, the actions they can take, and how enterprise data is governed and protected.

In September, updates across Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore, and Strands strengthened those foundations. New capabilities expanded model choice, made agent operations more efficient and measurable, and created more direct ways to connect AI applications with current business information.

Run faster agents and evaluate what matters

Build agents optimized for OpenAI models. Amazon Bedrock Managed Agents, powered by OpenAI, is now available in public preview, helping you build production-ready AI agents without sacrificing enterprise security. You can now use OpenAI models while keeping data within AWS, reuse existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions, and maintain full auditability through AWS CloudTrail. Durable sessions and built-in human approval workflows help reduce development overhead and mitigate risk.

Agents now start faster with less infrastructure overhead. The latest AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, has more efficient memory management and lower cold start latency for serverless agents, so you pay for actual usage rather than the peak memory. You can run agents faster at lower cost with pay-as-you-go pricing and no need to pre-provision capacity. Sessions scale to zero when idle and run in hardware-isolated environments.

Lower your token cost with frontier performance. Strands harness is a new open source agent harness that matches popular harnesses on accuracy while using 28 percent fewer tokens. You can spin up a production-ready agent in a single line of Python or TypeScript, with built-in context management, prompt caching, and memory, then deploy it anywhere.

Let your models make big decisions safely, locally. Strands Decider 2B is a small, open source, 2B-parameter decision model that picks between predefined options (instead of generating text), delivering answers in ~115ms locally. It’s optimized for agentic AI tasks like tool selection, routing, and guardrails, with all code, data, and weights available on GitHub and Hugging Face.

Find the right model for each workload

Choose from a broader set of OpenAI models for your everyday work. OpenAI’s Astra, Sol, and Luna models are now generally available on Amazon Bedrock, with options for demanding projects, recurring complex work, and high-volume tasks.

GPT-6 Astra is the flagship model for your most ambitious work, bringing deeper reasoning to complex decisions, document analysis, and software development with up to 1 million input tokens. It brings stronger reasoning and more precise judgment to complex business decisions, operates across software and files, and delivers professional-quality output aligned with organizational voice, templates, and standards. GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast adds a premium speed tier for GPT-6 Astra, built for workloads where speed matters most. It delivers up to 6x faster inference in the API, with up to 300 tokens per second.

Sol brings near-Astra intelligence to coding, computer use, and professional workloads that run frequently. Both GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Sol are available on Amazon Bedrock. GPT 6.1 Luna is designed for high-volume tasks such as extraction, summarization, classification, and routing. Together, they help you balance intelligence, latency, and cost across workloads.

Take on long-running coding and research with Claude. Model choices for Claude now include the latest versions to advance your coding and scientific work. Claude Fable 5.1 expands options for coding, scientific research, and enterprise workflows. Claude Opus 5.5 is built for agentic coding, knowledge work, and long-running tasks. It uses adaptive thinking to gauge how much reasoning a task needs and an effort parameter to set an upper bound on reasoning depth. Claude Sonnet 5.5 is a smarter, more efficient Sonnet suited to focused coding and knowledge work, delivering 30 percent lower cost per task at 30 percent faster speed than Claude Sonnet 5.

Reason through complexity with a broader model portfolio. Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 is now available on Amazon Bedrock. According to Moonshot AI, Kimi K3 is its most capable model and the first open model to reach 2.8 trillion parameters. With a 1-million-token context window, native vision, and built-in prompt caching, it helps you build smarter apps 2.5x faster at lower cost than previous versions.

xAI’s frontier models Grok 4.6 and Grok 4.7 offer a 500K token context window and support configurable reasoning effort and self-verification for more reliable long-running tasks.

Together, these additions give you more flexibility when matching models to your requirements such as context length, latency, throughput, and cost.

Get more control over your enterprise AI agents

Keep agent knowledge current. With new automatic sync scheduling in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you can now configure daily, weekly, and monthly refresh options for all native data-source connectors. As a result, your enterprise AI agents retrieve the latest information. The user-managed setup for SharePoint, OneDrive, and Confluence reduces reliance on admin-managed service accounts when you already have the access you need.

Connect more enterprise sources without maintaining custom ingestion pipelines. Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports ServiceNow, Confluence Data Center, Salesforce, and Zendesk as native connectors to handle data crawling, metadata extraction, and incremental sync automatically. These connectors reduce the amount of custom ingestion code you need to build and maintain support content, internal documentation, and operational knowledge.

Get started

Explore Amazon Bedrock, deploy agents with the AgentCore CLI, or build your first agent with the Strands Harness SDK.

Interested in learning how Amazon Bedrock can support your team? Connect with us to start the conversation.
